# Retinal vessel occlusion

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Ophthalmic surgery > Retinal vessel occlusion*

[Original Article Link](/library/HO0KFT)

---

## Summary

Retinal vessel occlusion is the complete or partial obstruction of retinal <u>arteries</u> or <u>veins</u>, most commonly due to <u>thromboembolism</u>. Depending on the extent and site of occlusion (central vessel or its branches), retinal vessel occlusion may be asymptomatic or manifest as sudden painless loss of <u>vision</u> in the affected <u>eye</u>. <u>Retinal artery occlusion</u> (RAO) is the blockage of the <u>central retinal artery</u> or its branches and is a form of <u>ischemic stroke</u>. <u>Central retinal artery occlusion</u> is characterized by sudden, painless unilateral loss of <u>vision</u> and a <u>relative afferent pupillary defect</u>. On <u>fundoscopy</u>, the <u>ischemic</u> <u>retina</u> appears pale and <u>edematous</u> with a cherry-red spot at the <u>fovea centralis</u>. <u>Branch retinal artery occlusion</u> manifests with <u>visual field</u> defects corresponding to the affected <u>artery</u> branch; fundoscopic findings of retinal <u>ischemia</u> are limited to the territory of the affected <u>artery</u> branch. Patients with acute, symptomatic RAO require urgent referral for <u>stroke</u> evaluation, possible <u>thrombolysis</u>, and assessment and treatment of underlying systemic disease (e.g., acute <u>stroke</u>, <u>carotid stenosis</u>, <u>giant cell arteritis</u>). <u>Retinal vein occlusion</u> (RVO), categorized as either <u>central retinal vein occlusion</u> or <u>branch retinal vein occlusion</u>, is more common than RAO and follows a milder course. Typical fundoscopic findings include <u>retinal hemorrhages</u>, <u>cotton wool spots</u>, <u>macular edema</u>, and <u>papilledema</u>, which result from increased venous pressure in the <u>retina</u>. Management of RVO focuses on treating complications (e.g., <u>macular edema</u>, <u>neovascularization</u>) to minimize <u>vision loss</u> and optimizing <u>modifiable risk factors</u>. Patients with RAO often experience irreversible loss of <u>vision</u>, while the prognosis is more favorable for RVO.

---

## Retinal artery occlusion

### Definition [[1]](/library/B_WzqL0)




* RAO is the partial or complete obstruction of retinal <u>arteries</u> causing retinal <u>ischemia</u>.

* Classification of RAO is based on the site of the occlusion.

* Central retinal artery occlusion (<u>CRAO</u>): obstruction of the <u>central retinal artery</u> after it branches from the <u>ophthalmic artery</u>

* Branch retinal artery occlusion (<u>BRAO</u>): obstruction of one of the four branches (superior, inferior, nasal, or temporal) of the <u>central retinal artery</u>





> [!TIP]
> RAO is a form of acute <u>ischemic stroke</u>. [[2]](/library/A-WR-L0)




### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* Age of onset: : > 60 years [[1]](/library/B_WzqL0)

* Sex: <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> [[1]](/library/B_WzqL0)

* <u>Incidence</u> of <u>CRAO</u>: rare  [[2]](/library/A-WR-L0)





> [!TIP]
> <u>BRAO</u> is more common than <u>CRAO</u>. However, symptomatic <u>CRAO</u> is more common than symptomatic <u>BRAO</u>. [[2]](/library/A-WR-L0)




#### <u>Risk factors</u> [[1]](/library/B_WzqL0)




<u>Risk factors</u> for thromboembolic RAO are similar to <u>ASCVD risk factors</u> and include:




* <u>Cigarette smoking</u>

* <u>Hypertension</u>

* <u>Hyperlipidemia</u>

* <u>Obesity</u>

* <u>Diabetes mellitus</u>

* Cardiac disease (e.g., <u>atrial fibrillation</u>)

* History of <u>amaurosis fugax</u> or other transient <u>ischemic</u> neurological symptoms





### Etiology [[1]](/library/B_WzqL0)[[2]](/library/A-WR-L0)[[3]](/library/KZdUco0)




* <u>Thromboembolism</u> (95% of cases)  

* Carotid <u>artery</u> <u>atherosclerosis</u> (most common)

* Cardiogenic embolism (e.g., due to <u>atrial fibrillation</u>, <u>valvular heart disease</u>, <u>infective endocarditis</u>)

* Retinal <u>artery</u> <u>thrombosis</u> due to <u>atherosclerosis</u>

* <u>Vasculitis</u>:  (5% of cases): e.g., <u>giant cell arteritis</u> (<u>GCA</u>)  [[1]](/library/B_WzqL0)[[2]](/library/A-WR-L0)

* Rare causes

* <u>Hypercoagulable state</u>

* Retinal <u>artery</u> vasospasm

* <u>Fibromuscular dysplasia</u>

* Complication of cosmetic facial injection





> [!NOTE]
> Thromboembolic occlusion most commonly occurs at the lamina cribrosa, where the <u>central retinal artery</u> narrows as it pierces the dural sheath of the <u>optic nerve</u>. [[4]](/library/R0dlfo0)[[5]](/library/qZdCco0)




![Central retinal artery occlusion](media/n7jcmbdhvg6j5pia3k2g5tts.jpg)

Central retinal artery occlusion




### Clinical features [[1]](/library/B_WzqL0)




* Sudden, painless unilateral loss of <u>vision</u>

* Features of cerebral <u>stroke</u> may be present.  [[1]](/library/B_WzqL0)[[6]](/library/JZdsco0)

* Features of the underlying etiology may be present.





### Management




* Refer all patients with suspected RAO to an emergency department or a <u>stroke center</u> immediately.  [[1]](/library/B_WzqL0)[[2]](/library/A-WR-L0)

* Confirm the diagnosis with <u>comprehensive eye examination</u>; consider retinal imaging.

* Perform concurrent assessment for underlying serious underlying etiologies (<u>ischemic stroke</u>, <u>GCA</u>).

* Treat underlying causes and optimize <u>modifiable risk factors</u>.

* Follow up patients regularly to assess for complications.





> [!WARNING]
> Acute, symptomatic RAO is an ophthalmologic and medical emergency. Do not delay management as permanent retinal damage occurs quickly and there is a high risk of serious comorbid illness (e.g., cerebral <u>stroke</u>, cardiovascular disease). [[1]](/library/B_WzqL0)[[2]](/library/A-WR-L0)[[6]](/library/JZdsco0)




#### Diagnostics [[1]](/library/B_WzqL0)[[2]](/library/A-WR-L0)




##### <u>Comprehensive eye examination</u>




| Examination findings in central vs. <u>branch retinal artery occlusion</u> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | <br><u>CRAO</u> [[1]](/library/B_WzqL0)[[2]](/library/A-WR-L0)<br> | <br><u>BRAO</u> [[5]](/library/qZdCco0)[[7]](/library/pZdLco0)<br> |
| Characteristics of <u>vision loss</u> | <br>* Sudden, painless unilateral loss of <u>vision</u> (often described as a “descending curtain”)<br><br> | <br>* Sudden onset of <u>visual field</u> defects (<u>scotomas</u>) in the affected <u>eye</u><br><br> |
| <u>Visual acuity</u> | <br><br>* Usually 20/200 or worse<br><br>* Central <u>vision</u> is preserved in some patients.  [[1]](/library/B_WzqL0)[[2]](/library/A-WR-L0)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Depends on site of occlusion<br><br>* Typically 20/40 or better<br><br><br> |
| <u>Relative afferent pupillary defect</u> | <br>* Present<br><br> | <br>* Absent<br><br> |
| Dilated <u>fundoscopic examination</u> | <br><br>* Diffuse retinal <u>ischemia</u><br><br>* Gray-white (cloudy) discoloration of the entire <u>retina</u><br><br>* Cherry-red spot at the <u>fovea centralis</u><br><br>* Slow segmented blood flow (box-carring) in all retinal <u>arterioles</u> in the acute phase<br><br>* Narrowing of all retinal vessels<br><br>* <u>Retinal emboli</u> (i.e., <u>Hollenhorst plaque</u>, <u>platelet</u>-<u>fibrin</u> <u>emboli</u>, calcific <u>emboli</u>)<br><br>* Rarely visible (< 10% of <u>CRAO</u>)  [[2]](/library/A-WR-L0)<br><br>* Presence suggests thromboembolic etiology  [[1]](/library/B_WzqL0)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Segmental retinal <u>ischemia</u><br><br>* Gray-white discoloration of the retinal quadrant supplied by the affected vessel<br><br>* Box-carring in retinal <u>arterioles</u> of the affected quadrant in the acute phase<br><br>* Narrow retinal vessels in the affected retinal quadrant<br><br>* <u>Retinal emboli</u>: often visible (∼ 65% of <u>BRAO</u>) [[7]](/library/pZdLco0)<br><br><br> |





> [!WARNING]
> The classic <u>CRAO</u> findings of a gray-white, <u>edematous</u> <u>retina</u> and a cherry-red spot may take several hours to develop. <u>CRAO</u> should be suspected if a patient presents with sudden, painless <u>vision loss</u> and a <u>relative afferent pupillary defect</u>, even if the initial <u>fundoscopic examination</u> appears normal. [[1]](/library/B_WzqL0)[[2]](/library/A-WR-L0)

##### Retinal imaging [[1]](/library/B_WzqL0)[[2]](/library/A-WR-L0)




* Indications

* Diagnostic uncertainty

* Assessment of severity [[8]](/library/jTd_q60)

* Options

* <u>Optical coherence tomography</u>

* Fundus <u>fluorescein angiography</u>

* <u>Electroretinogram</u>





#### Assessment for underlying etiology [[2]](/library/A-WR-L0)[[4]](/library/R0dlfo0)[[8]](/library/jTd_q60)




* Further assessment depends on patient age and clinical features.

* For patients ≥ 50 years of age, assess for:

* <u>Thromboembolism</u>  [[2]](/library/A-WR-L0)

* <u>Symptoms of giant cell arteritis</u>; if present, initiate <u>treatment of GCA</u> with high-dose <u>steroids</u> before obtaining diagnostic studies.

* For patients < 50 years of age:

* <u>Risk factors</u> for vascular disease: Assess for suspected <u>thromboembolism</u>.

* No <u>risk factors</u> for vascular disease: Assess for <u>hypercoagulability</u>.





| <br>Assessment for underlying etiology of RAO [[2]](/library/A-WR-L0)[[4]](/library/R0dlfo0)[[8]](/library/jTd_q60)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| Suspected etiology | Recommended studies |
| Thromboemolism | <br><br>* CT head<br><br>* <u>Carotid duplex ultrasound</u><br><br>* <u>Echocardiogram</u><br><br>* <u>ECG</u> [[9]](/library/HLWK_N0)<br><br>* <u>Fasting blood glucose</u> and <u>cholesterol</u> levels<br><br>* <u>Ambulatory cardiac monitoring</u> (if <u>atrial fibrillation</u> is suspected)  [[2]](/library/A-WR-L0)<br><br><br> |
| <u>GCA</u> | <br><br>* <u>Inflammatory markers</u><br><br>* <u>Temporal artery</u> imaging and/or <u>biopsy</u><br><br>* See “<u>Diagnostics for GCA</u>.”<br><br><br> |
| <u>Hypercoagulable state</u> | <br><br>* <u>Coagulation studies</u><br><br>* Hypercoagulation screen<br><br>* <u>Vasculitis</u> screen<br><br>* <u>Peripheral blood smear</u><br><br><br> |





#### Treatment [[1]](/library/B_WzqL0)[[2]](/library/A-WR-L0)




* Management is aimed at identifying and treating the underlying cause.

* Specialists may consider <u>thrombolysis</u>.  [[2]](/library/A-WR-L0)[[10]](/library/SZdyao0)

* To prevent recurrence of <u>CRAO</u> or other forms of <u>ischemic stroke</u>:  [[1]](/library/B_WzqL0)

* Start <u>primary prevention of stroke</u> to optimize <u>modifiable risk factors</u>.

* Educate patients on symptoms of <u>stroke</u> and the importance of seeking early treatment.

* Arrange regular follow-up with ophthalmology to optimize <u>vision</u> and assess for complications (e.g., <u>neovascularization</u>). [[2]](/library/A-WR-L0)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Conservative measures</u> such as ocular massage, <u>anterior chamber paracentesis</u>, <u>IOP</u>-lowering medications (e.g., <u>timolol</u> and <u>acetazolamide</u>), and <u>vasodilation</u> are controversial, as studies show no evidence of <u>efficacy</u> but some evidence of harm. [[1]](/library/B_WzqL0)[[2]](/library/A-WR-L0)




### Differential diagnoses [[2]](/library/A-WR-L0)




* Other causes of sudden, painless, unilateral <u>vision loss</u>, e.g.:

* <u>Retinal detachment</u>

* Intraocular hemorrhage

* Optic neuropathy

* Other causes of a cherry-red spot on <u>fundoscopy</u>, e.g.:

* <u>Tay-Sachs disease</u>

* <u>Niemann-Pick disease</u>





### Prognosis




* <u>CRAO</u>: severe, often irreversible loss of <u>vision</u>  [[2]](/library/A-WR-L0)

* <u>BRAO</u>: often irreversible <u>visual field</u> defects (depending on which branch of the retinal <u>artery</u> is affected)

* Individuals with RAO are at increased risk for subsequent <u>stroke</u>, <u>myocardial infarction</u>, and <u>death</u>. [[6]](/library/JZdsco0)

## Retinal vein occlusion

### Definition [[11]](/library/qJbCEu)




* RVO is the partial or complete obstruction of a retinal <u>vein</u>.

* Classification of RVO is based on the site of the obstruction.  [[11]](/library/qJbCEu)

* Central retinal vein occlusion (<u>CRVO</u>): obstruction of the <u>central retinal vein</u> at or <u>proximal</u> to the lamina cribrosa

* Branch retinal vein occlusion (<u>BRVO</u>): obstruction of a branch or tributary of the <u>central retinal vein</u>





> [!TIP]
> The terms "<u>ischemic</u> RVO" and "nonischemic RVO" are no longer preferred because all forms of RVO show signs of <u>ischemia</u>. [[11]](/library/qJbCEu)




### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* Age of onset: > 40 years [[11]](/library/qJbCEu)

* Sex: <u>♂</u> = <u>♀</u> [[12]](/library/nad7Oo0)





> [!NOTE]
> RVO is the second most common vascular disease of the <u>retina</u> (after <u>diabetic retinopathy</u>) and is much more common than RAO. [[11]](/library/qJbCEu)[[13]](/library/madVOo0)




### Etiology [[11]](/library/qJbCEu)[[13]](/library/madVOo0)




RVO is typically caused by <u>thrombosis</u> within a retinal <u>vein</u>. <u>Risk factors</u> for RVO include conditions associated with <u>atherosclerosis</u> and thrombogenesis, e.g.:




* Major <u>risk factors</u>

* History of RVO

* Older age

* <u>Hypertension</u>

* <u>Atherosclerosis</u> (systemic and/or retinal <u>artery</u>)  [[11]](/library/qJbCEu)[[13]](/library/madVOo0)

* <u>Hyperlipidemia</u>

* <u>Diabetes mellitus</u>

* Minor <u>risk factors</u>

* <u>Hypercoagulable states</u>

* <u>Glaucoma</u>

* <u>Vasculitides</u>





### Clinical features [[11]](/library/qJbCEu)




* <u>CRVO</u>: sudden, painless unilateral loss or blurring of <u>vision</u>

* <u>BRVO</u>: variable presentation

* May be asymptomatic if the <u>macula</u> is spared

* <u>Floaters</u>

* Sudden, painless <u>visual field</u> defect





### Diagnostics [[11]](/library/qJbCEu)




* RVO is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> based on history and findings on a <u>comprehensive eye examination</u>.

* Refer to ophthalmology for diagnostic confirmation and management.

* Assess for underlying etiology (e.g., screening for <u>modifiable ASCVD risk factors</u>, <u>thrombophilia</u>, <u>vasculitis</u>). [[11]](/library/qJbCEu)[[14]](/library/5Tdir60)





#### <u>Eye examination</u>




| <br>Clinical features of central vs. <u>branch retinal vein occlusion</u> [[11]](/library/qJbCEu)[[15]](/library/qadClo0)[[16]](/library/ATdRt60)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | <br><u>CRVO</u> <br> | <u>BRVO</u> |
| Characteristics of <u>vision loss</u> | <br>* Sudden, painless unilateral loss of <u>vision</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Sudden, painless unilateral <u>visual field</u> defects (<u>scotomas</u>)<br><br>* May be asymptomatic if the <u>macula</u> is spared<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Visual acuity</u> [[5]](/library/qZdCco0)<br> | <br>* Usually 20/200 or worse<br><br> | <br>* 20/40 or better<br><br> |
| <u>Relative afferent pupillary defect</u> | <br>* Present<br><br> | <br>* Absent<br><br> |
| Dilated <u>fundoscopic examination</u> | <br><br>* <u>Dot-blot hemorrhages</u> and/or flame-shaped hemorrhages in all four retinal quadrants and dilated <u>tortuous</u> retinal <u>veins</u> (blood and thunder appearance)<br><br>* Cotton wool spots<br><br>* Characterized by yellow-white deposits on the <u>retina</u><br><br>* Caused by swelling of retinal nerve fibers due to <u>ischemia</u><br><br>* <u>Macular edema</u><br><br>* <u>Papilledema</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* In the retinal quadrant or hemisphere drained by the affected <u>vein</u>:<br><br>* <u>Dot-blot hemorrhages</u> and/or flame-shaped hemorrhages<br><br>* <u>Cotton wool spots</u><br><br>* Depending on the affected <u>vein</u>, <u>macular edema</u> may be present.<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> Features on <u>fundoscopy</u> in acute RVO result from increased venous pressure. In <u>CRVO</u>, these features affect the whole <u>retina</u>, while in <u>BRVO</u>, they are segmented and restricted to the affected retinal area.

#### Retinal imaging [[11]](/library/qJbCEu)




The following modalities can be used to determine the extent of retinal <u>ischemia</u> and <u>macular edema</u>, and to assess response to therapy.




* <u>Fluorescein angiography</u>

* <u>Optical coherence tomography</u>

* Fundus photography





![Fluorescein angiography in ischemic branch retinal vein occlusion](media/qiw1y3e139v2ud6pg2ebl8ct.jpg)

Fluorescein angiography in ischemic branch retinal vein occlusion

![Cystoid macular edema](media/bv9linzj3di2bf121c91hsqv.jpg)

Cystoid macular edema

![Cystoid macular edema](media/hgn1quvr1qseot00wkaxxva3.jpg)

Cystoid macular edema




### Management [[11]](/library/qJbCEu)




* There are currently no established treatments to reverse RVO; treatment is that of underlying etiology.  [[11]](/library/qJbCEu)[[17]](/library/zddrsK0)

* Treat associated <u>macular edema</u> with:

* Preferred: <u>intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy</u>

* Alternative: intravitreal <u>steroids</u> (e.g., <u>dexamethasone</u>)

* Ongoing management is shared between ophthalmology and <u>internal medicine</u> and/or primary care. [[11]](/library/qJbCEu)

* <u>Internal medicine</u> and/or primary care optimize <u>modifiable risk factors</u> to prevent recurrence.

* Ophthalmology screens for and manages complications (e.g., provides peripheral <u>panretinal photocoagulation</u> for <u>neovascularization</u>).  [[11]](/library/qJbCEu)[[18]](/library/MTdMr60)





### Complications [[11]](/library/qJbCEu)




Release of vasoproliferative substances (e.g., <u>VEGF</u>) from the <u>ischemic</u> <u>retina</u> causes:




* <u>Neovascularization of the iris</u> (<u>rubeosis iridis</u>) → <u>neovascular glaucoma</u>

* <u>Neovascularization</u> of the <u>retina</u>  → <u>vitreous hemorrhage</u> → <u>retinal detachment</u>





> [!TIP]
> 25% of patients with <u>CRVO</u> develop <u>neovascularization</u>. [[11]](/library/qJbCEu)




### Prognosis




* Depends on the site of occlusion (<u>distal</u> better than <u>proximal</u>) and degree of occlusion (partial occlusion better than complete occlusion, <u>BRVO</u> better than <u>CRVO</u>) [[11]](/library/qJbCEu)

* Patients with RVO have an increased risk of <u>all-cause mortality</u> and cardiovascular events. [[19]](/library/-ddDsK0)

## Amaurosis fugax

* Definition: sudden, painless loss of <u>vision</u> that lasts for seconds to minutes and is followed by spontaneous recovery (mostly unilateral)

* Cause: retinal <u>ischemia</u> following transient occlusion of the <u>central retinal artery</u> by microemboli

* Cardiovascular causes (<u>atherosclerosis</u>, <u>carotid artery stenosis</u>, cardiac <u>thrombi</u>)

* <u>Vasculitis</u> (e.g., <u>temporal arteritis</u>, <u>lupus</u> erythematosus, <u>polyarteritis nodosa</u>)

* Diagnostics: see “<u>Diagnostics for TIA</u>.”

* Treatment
* Although <u>amaurosis fugax</u> is <u>self-limiting</u>, it is a harbinger of more serious conditions. Therefore, <u>perimetry</u> and treatment of the underlying cause are essential:

* Reduction of <u>cardiovascular risk factors</u> (e.g., low-dose <u>aspirin</u> therapy)

* In the case of <u>temporal arteritis</u>: high-dose <u>glucocorticoid</u> therapy

* Complications

* RAO

* <u>Transient ischemic attacks</u> (<u>TIAs</u>)

* <u>Stroke</u>

---
